lesson.title: The real transformer: losses, tests and efficiency

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the copper-loss bar fall from 400 W to match the flat 100 W iron-loss bar, and efficiency peak, while the flux bar holds still, when you drag the load from 100% to 50%.
interactive.title: Where the watts go
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Thirteen small screens on one picture, with Back and Continue. Five show an idea and eight ask you to try it.

The picture. A 10 kVA, 440 V to 115 V transformer, say, drawn as its approximate equivalent circuit, seen from the 440 V side. On the left, a 440 V, 60 Hz supply with a wattmeter and an ammeter. Across it, the shunt branch for the core: a resistor beside a coil, labelled Core. In line after it, the series branch for the windings: 0.77 Ω of resistance and 0.58 Ω of leakage reactance, labelled Windings, with its current in amps beside it. Then the last lesson's ideal transformer, 880 turns to 230, with a flux bar on its core, and the load. A branch carrying current is drawn in ink, one carrying none or almost none faint. Below, two loss bars on one scale, Iron loss and Copper loss, in W. Under them, a plot of efficiency, 88% to 97%, against load, 0 to 125%: a dot on the curve, a dashed line at its 50% peak. At light load the curve drops off the bottom. In either test the plot fades, since nothing is delivered.

The controls, each shown only where a screen uses it. A load slider, 0 to 125% in steps of 5, opening at 100. A power factor switch, 1.0 or 0.8 lagging, opening at 1.0. A test selector, On load, Open-circuit test or Short-circuit test, opening On load. Its buttons wrap onto two rows on a phone. In either test the load slider is greyed out.

The rules. Full-load current at 440 V: 10,000 ÷ 440 = 22.7 A. Load fraction x = slider ÷ 100. Output = 10,000 × x × power factor, in W. Iron loss = 100 W, fixed by the flux, which the supply holds at the last lesson's 1.88 mWb. Copper loss = 400 × x², in W: it is I²R, and the current follows the load. The 0.77 Ω gives 400 W at 22.7 A. Efficiency = output ÷ (output + both losses), in %, and 0 at no load, where nothing is delivered. It peaks where the copper loss equals the iron loss, at x = √(100 ÷ 400) = 0.5, at either power factor.

The tests. Open circuit: the secondary open on 440 V. Only the shunt branch carries current, say 0.5 A. Flux 1.88 mWb, wattmeter 100 W, copper loss 0.0 W. Short circuit: a link across the secondary, the supply down to 22.0 V, driving 22.7 A through the series branch's 0.97 Ω. Nearly all the current takes that branch. The core's branch, on 5% of the voltage, takes only a trickle. Wattmeter 400 W. Flux 1.88 × 22.0 ÷ 440 = 0.09 mWb. The model's iron loss goes with the voltage squared, a sketch: 100 × (22.0 ÷ 440)² = 0.25 W.

The readouts, wrapping onto two rows on a phone, to one decimal place: Load, %; Output, kW; Iron loss, W; Copper loss, W; Efficiency, %. In a test: Supply voltage, V; Supply current, A; Wattmeter, W, whole watts. The flux bar reads in mWb, two decimal places.

Screen 1, try it, a recall, typed. "A curve's height is y = 6x − x². Its slope is 6 − 2x. At what x does it reach its top?" Typed, no unit, whole numbers: answer 3, want "3". Slips: 6, "That is where the height is back to zero. The top is where the slope is zero."; 9, "That is the height at the top. The question asks for x." Hint otherwise: "At the top the slope is zero. Solve 6 − 2x = 0." Why: "6 − 2x = 0 gives x = 3. The height there is 18 − 9 = 9. You find the top of an efficiency curve the same way." The picture, plot and readouts are hidden on this screen. A right Check says "Right: the slope is zero at x = 3." Read: "The curve y = 6x − x² has slope 6 − 2x. At what x is its top?"

Screen 2, show. The load slider to drag. The words: "A real transformer is the ideal one plus two branches. The ideal one lost nothing. The shunt branch sits across the supply and stands for the core. It takes the small current that magnetises the core. It also takes the iron loss, from hysteresis and eddy currents. The series branch sits in line with the load and stands for the windings. Its resistance wastes power as heat. Its reactance stands for leakage: flux that misses the other winding. Drag the load. Only the series branch's current changes." Read: "A real transformer is the ideal one plus two branches. The shunt branch sits across the supply and stands for the core. The series branch sits in line with the load and stands for the windings. Only the series branch's current changes with the load." Still: on load, 50%.

Screen 3, try it, typed. "This transformer's windings lose 400 W at full load. What do they lose at 75% load?" Typed, in W, whole numbers: answer 225, want "225 W". The copper loss readout shows ? until Check. Slips: 300, "That scales it straight with the load. The loss goes with the current squared."; 400, "That is the full-load figure. At 75% load the current is 0.75 of full." Hint otherwise: "Copper loss = 400 × (load fraction)²." Why: "0.75² = 0.5625. 400 × 0.5625 = 225 W." A right Check sets the load to 75%. Read: "This transformer's windings lose 400 W at full load. What do they lose at 75% load?"

Screen 4, show. The load slider to drag. The words: "Copper loss grows with the load, but iron loss stays put. Drag the load and watch the two bars. The copper loss is I²R, so it goes with the current squared. Full load gives 400 W. Half load gives a quarter, 100 W. Here the iron loss stays at 100 W at every load.[^1] It depends on the flux, and the flux bar stays at 1.88 mWb. The supply's voltage holds the flux. The primary cancels the load's ampere-turns. So more load means more current, not more flux." Read: "The copper loss grows with the square of the load. It is 400 W at full load and 100 W at half. The iron loss stays at 100 W, because the supply holds the flux at 1.88 mWb." Still: on load, 100%.

Screen 5, try it, typed. The picture: on load, 50%. "At half load this transformer's iron loss is 100 W. The load rises to full. What is its iron loss now?" Typed, in W, whole numbers: answer 100, want "100 W". The iron loss readout shows ? until Check. Slips: 400, "That grows it with the square, like the copper loss. But the iron loss follows the flux."; 200, "That doubles it with the load. The load does not move the flux." Hint otherwise: "What sets the flux, the load or the supply?" Why: "The supply still holds the flux at 1.88 mWb. Same flux, same iron loss: 100 W. The copper loss grows from 100 W to 400 W." A right Check moves the load to 100%. Read: "At half load this transformer's iron loss is 100 W. The load rises to full. What is its iron loss now?"

Screen 6, show. The load slider and the power factor switch. The words: "Efficiency is output ÷ input. The input is the output plus both losses. At full load and unity power factor, the load takes 10,000 W. The losses are 100 + 400 = 500 W. So the efficiency is 10,000 ÷ 10,500 = 95.2%. Now switch to 0.8 power factor. The load is set in kVA, so the current is still 22.7 A. So the losses stay the same. That is why the plate gives kVA. But only 8000 W comes out. So the efficiency falls to 94.1%." Read: "At full load and unity power factor, 10,000 W comes out and 500 W is lost. That is 95.2%. At 0.8 power factor, only 8000 W comes out for the same losses. That is 94.1%." Still: on load, 100%, power factor 1.0.

Screen 7, try it, typed. "The same transformer runs at half load, unity power factor. What is its efficiency?" Typed, in %, one decimal place: answer 96.2, want "96.2%". The efficiency readout shows ? until Check. Slips: 90.9, "That uses the full-load copper loss. At half load it is a quarter of that, 100 W."; 94.3, "That halves the copper loss. It goes with the square, so it quarters." Hint otherwise: "Output 5000 W. Losses: 100 W iron, plus 400 × 0.5² copper." Why: "Copper loss = 400 × 0.25 = 100 W. So the losses are 200 W in all. 5000 ÷ 5200 = 96.2%. That beats the 95.2% at full load." A right Check sets the load to 50%. Read: "The same transformer runs at half load, unity power factor. What is its efficiency?"

Screen 8, show. The load slider to drag. The words: "Efficiency peaks at 50% load, where both loss bars read 100 W. Drag the load and watch the dot. Call the load fraction x. The losses are 100 + 400x². Divide by the output, which grows as x. The loss per watt out goes as 100 ÷ x + 400x. Least loss per watt means highest efficiency. It is lowest where its slope, 400 − 100 ÷ x², is zero. That needs 400x² = 100. So copper loss equals iron loss. Then x = √(100 ÷ 400) = 0.5." Read: "Efficiency peaks at 50% load, where the copper loss equals the 100 W iron loss. Peak load = √(iron loss ÷ full-load copper loss)." Still: on load, 50%.

Screen 9, try it, typed. The plot and readouts are hidden, since they show the first transformer. "Another transformer has 64 W of iron loss and 400 W of copper loss at full load. At what load is it most efficient?" Typed, in %, whole numbers: answer 40, want "40%". Slips: 16, "That is 64 ÷ 400. Take its square root."; 250, "That is upside down. Put the iron loss on top." Hint otherwise: "Peak load = √(iron loss ÷ full-load copper loss)." Why: "64 ÷ 400 = 0.16, and √0.16 = 0.4. So the peak is at 40%. Check: 400 × 0.4² = 64 W of copper loss, equal to the iron loss." Read: "A transformer has 64 W of iron loss and 400 W of full-load copper loss. At what load is it most efficient?"

Screen 10, show. The test selector to switch. The words: "Two tests measure the two losses. The open-circuit test leaves the secondary open. The primary gets its full 440 V. The flux is full, but only a small current flows. A small current wastes almost nothing in the windings. So the wattmeter reads the iron loss, 100 W.[^2] The short-circuit test puts a link across the secondary. You raise the voltage from zero until rated current flows. Now the current is full, but the voltage is only 22.0 V. So the wattmeter reads the copper loss, 400 W.[^3]" Read: "With the secondary open at rated voltage, the wattmeter reads the iron loss, 100 W. With it shorted at rated current, on 22.0 V, it reads the copper loss, 400 W." Still: Short-circuit test.

Screen 11, try it, typed. The picture: the short-circuit test, its flux readout ? until Check. "The short-circuit test drives 22.7 A with 22.0 V on the primary. At 440 V the flux peaks at 1.88 mWb. What does it peak at in this test?" Typed, in mWb, two decimal places: answer 0.09, accepting 0.094, want "0.09 mWb". Slips: 1.88, "Rated current flows, but the voltage sets the flux."; 37.6, "The voltage is 20 times lower, so the flux is too." Hint otherwise: "The flux follows the voltage. 22.0 V is 5% of 440 V." Why: "1.88 × 22.0 ÷ 440 = 0.09 mWb, 5% of normal. So the iron loss almost vanishes. The wattmeter reads the copper loss alone." Read: "At 440 V the flux peaks at 1.88 mWb. What does it peak at in the short-circuit test, on 22.0 V?"

Screen 12, try it, the first of two mixed puzzles, typed. The plot and readouts are hidden, since they show the first transformer. "A 100 kVA transformer's open-circuit test reads 500 W. Its short-circuit test at rated current reads 2000 W. It feeds a steady 20 kVA load at unity power factor. What is its efficiency?" Typed, in %, one decimal place: answer 97.2, want "97.2%". Slips: 88.9, "That uses the full-load copper loss. At 20% load it is 0.2² of that."; 95.7, "That scales the copper loss straight with the load. It goes with the square."; 99.6, "That leaves out the iron loss. It is there at every load.". Hint otherwise: "Load fraction 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2. Copper loss = 2000 × 0.2². Add the 500 W iron loss." Why: "Copper loss = 2000 × 0.2² = 80 W. So 500 W of the 580 W lost is iron loss. 20,000 ÷ 20,580 = 97.2%. At its 50% peak it would give 98.0%. A big transformer on a light load wastes mostly iron loss." Read: "A 100 kVA transformer tests at 500 W open circuit and 2000 W short circuit. It feeds a steady 20 kVA at unity power factor. What is its efficiency?"

Screen 13, try it, the second mixed puzzle. "You want to measure a transformer's iron loss. How do you set up the test?" Four choices, in this order: "Secondary shorted, rated current"; "Secondary shorted, rated voltage"; "Secondary open, rated current"; "Secondary open, rated voltage". Right, the fourth. Hint for the first: "That is the short-circuit test. Its low voltage gives little flux. So it reads the copper loss." Hint for the second: "Full voltage on a shorted secondary is a dead short. Here it would drive 20 times rated current." Hint for the third: "The iron loss follows the flux. The voltage sets the flux. So set the voltage." Why: "The iron loss needs the full flux, and rated voltage gives it. With the secondary open, only a small current flows. So the copper loss is too small to count." Read: "You want to measure a transformer's iron loss. How do you set up the test?"

The finish. The words: "The supply holds the flux, so the iron loss barely moves with the load. The copper loss grows with the square of the load. Efficiency peaks where the two are equal. The open-circuit test reads the iron loss. The short-circuit test reads the copper loss. The 22.0 V it needs, 5% of rated, is called the impedance voltage. Next: what that 5% means for the voltage under load."
interactive.ignores: The circuit is the approximate one. It puts the shunt branch right across the supply. So the flux and the iron loss stay exactly fixed under load. In a real transformer, the series branch's drop lowers the core's voltage very slightly. So both dip very slightly too. The iron loss is fixed only while the supply's voltage and frequency are. Here the open-circuit test's small current does not pass the series branch. So the copper loss reads 0.0 W. Through the 0.77 Ω it would add only 0.19 W. The windings' resistance is held fixed. Real copper's resistance rises as it warms. Loss in the tank and fittings is left out. The load is single-phase. Every current and voltage is rms. The losses are larger than a good transformer's. That makes the bars easy to see.

explain.text:
A real transformer loses a little of the power it passes on. It loses it in two places. The core loses a fixed amount whenever the transformer is energised. The windings lose more as the load grows, with the square of the current. Two tests measure the two losses. The efficiency peaks at the load where they are equal.

Start with the core. Hysteresis and eddy currents heat the iron every cycle. How much depends on the flux. The supply's voltage holds the flux. The primary cancels whatever ampere-turns the load adds. So the flux barely changes from no load to full, and nor does this [[iron loss]]. The windings are different. They are copper with resistance, so they waste I²R. Double the current and this [[copper loss]] goes up four times. So the iron loss is there whenever the transformer is energised, whatever the load. But the copper loss grows with the square of the load.[^1] Some flux also leaks round each winding without threading the other. The [[equivalent circuit]] draws all this as the ideal transformer plus two branches. A shunt branch across the supply stands for the core. A series branch of resistance and leakage reactance stands for the windings.

Efficiency is output ÷ (output + losses). Take a 10 kVA transformer with 100 W of iron loss and 400 W of copper loss at full load. At full load and unity power factor, it gives 10,000 W and loses 500 W. So its efficiency is 10,000 ÷ 10,500 = 95.2%. At half load the copper loss is a quarter, 100 W. It gives 5000 W and loses 200 W. That is 96.2%, better than at full load. To find the peak, call the load fraction x. The losses for each watt delivered go as 100 ÷ x + 400x. The first part falls as the load grows. The second part rises. The total is lowest where its slope is zero: 400 − 100 ÷ x² = 0. That gives 400x² = 100. So at the peak, the copper loss equals the iron loss. Here x = √(100 ÷ 400) = 0.5, half load.

Two tests measure the two losses. The open-circuit test leaves the secondary open and puts rated voltage on the primary. The flux is full but the current is small. So the wattmeter reads the iron loss.[^2] The short-circuit test measures the copper loss, with a link shorting the secondary.[^3] You raise the voltage from zero until rated current flows. Here that takes only 22.0 V, 5% of 440 V. The current is full but the flux is tiny. So the wattmeter reads the copper loss. This picture is simplified. In a real transformer, the flux dips very slightly under load. So does the iron loss. A good transformer can lose as little as 1% of the power it passes on.[^4] This example's losses are larger, to make the bars easy to see. **The iron loss stays almost the same at every load while the transformer is energised. The copper loss grows with the square of the load.[^1] The efficiency peaks where the two are equal.**

analogy.text: Think of a long sub-main feeding a workshop board. The board's indicator lamps, meter and controls draw the same small power whenever it is live. The load makes no difference. The sub-main's own resistance wastes I²R. That goes up four times when the current doubles. At light load, the fixed draw is most of the waste. At heavy load, the cable's heat is. The share wasted is smallest at the load where the two are equal.
analogy.breaks: The board's standing load is separate kit you could switch off. A transformer's iron loss comes from its own core. It stops only when you de-energise the transformer. Also, a sub-main passes power on at the same voltage, less its drop. A transformer changes the voltage. And the board's lamps and meter do a job, so theirs is a standing draw. A transformer's iron loss does nothing useful.

practice.text:
**Safe way first:**
- In the open-circuit test, treat the open secondary as live. It sits at its full rated voltage.
- In the short-circuit test, start the supply at zero. Bring it up slowly while you watch the ammeter. Stop at rated current. Full voltage on a shorted secondary is a dead short.

**Steps:**
- Get the rating in kVA. Take the iron loss from the open-circuit test. Take the full-load copper loss from the short-circuit test.
- Work out the load fraction x: the load in kVA ÷ the rating.
- Copper loss = full-load copper loss × x².
- Output = rating × x × power factor.
- Efficiency = output ÷ (output + iron loss + copper loss).
- Peak load = √(iron loss ÷ full-load copper loss).

**Rules of thumb:** The iron loss runs whenever the transformer is energised, even with nothing connected. The copper loss quarters when the load halves. Efficiency peaks where the two are equal. A lower power factor gives the same losses for fewer watts. So the efficiency falls. An oversized transformer on a light load wastes mostly iron loss.

**Worked example:** A 10 kVA transformer tests at 100 W open circuit and 400 W short circuit. At full load and unity power factor, it loses 100 + 400 = 500 W. So its efficiency is 10,000 ÷ 10,500 = 95.2%. At half load the copper loss is 400 × 0.5² = 100 W. So the efficiency is 5000 ÷ 5200 = 96.2%. That is the peak, since √(100 ÷ 400) = 0.5. At full load and 0.8 power factor, it gives 8000 W for the same 500 W. That is 94.1%. Left energised all day with no load, it still burns 100 W × 24 h = 2.4 kWh.

**Common mistakes**
- Expecting a heavy load to raise the iron loss. The supply sets the flux, not the load.
- Scaling the copper loss straight with the load. It goes with the square.
- Taking the short-circuit test's reading as the total loss. It is the copper loss at rated current only.
- Forgetting the iron loss at light load. It is why efficiency falls away as the load drops.

checks.label: A no-load loss is present whenever the transformer is energised and is independent of the load level, and the load loss goes with the loading squared
An open-circuit test measures the iron loss under no-load conditions: on 440 V with the secondary open, 0.5 A flows and the wattmeter reads the 100 W iron loss
The short-circuit test determines the copper loss by short-circuiting the secondary at full-load current: 22.0 V drives 22.7 A, and the wattmeter reads 400 W
The series branch: 0.77 Ω gives 400 W at the full-load 22.7 A, and with 0.58 Ω of reactance makes 0.97 Ω; the flux is 1.88 mWb at 440 V
Efficiency: 95.2% at full load and 96.2% at half load at unity power factor, 94.1% and 95.2% at 0.8, and 0 at no load
Efficiency peaks at 50% load at both power factors, where the copper loss equals the iron loss, and falls below 88% at light load
The flux holds at 1.88 mWb at every load, while the copper-loss bar is four times the iron-loss bar at full load and equal at half load
Before a Check the copper loss, iron loss, efficiency and flux show ?; a right Check moves the load to 75%, 100% and 50%, and shows 225.0 W, 100.0 W, 96.2% and 0.09 mWb
Only the windings' branch changes with the load: at no load it is faint, and the core's branch carries current at every load; its label reads 22.7 A at full load, 11.4 A at half

applied.problem: The closing bold line says the iron loss is "fixed" while energised, but the same paragraph says it dips slightly under load and it also moves with supply voltage and frequency; read alone on review it overstates the source's "independent of the load level".

In the short-circuit test the shunt branch sits across 22.0 V and makes the shown 0.25 W iron loss, so "Only that branch carries current" contradicts the model; screen 4's [^1] sat on a flux claim its quote does not make; the finish's "fixed" is narrowed as in the explanation.

The lesson energises the 440 V side for both tests; a specialist would add that real open-circuit tests are usually fed from the low-voltage side and short-circuit tests from the high-voltage side, with the same losses read, so the model's choice is not taken as practice.
"The load ÷ the rating" lets the load be taken in kW, which gives the wrong x at 0.8 power factor (the next step multiplies by power factor again); the load must be in kVA, like the rating.
